title: WPA3
summary: WPA3 is the current generation of the Wi-Fi Protected Access certification for wireless networks, introduced to replace the pre-shared key handshake that made WPA2 vulnerable to offline guessing of captured handshakes. Its central mechanism is Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, a password-authenticated key exchange in which both sides prove knowledge of the passphrase without ever sending it, and the resulting session key is bound to that exchange; a captured handshake therefore cannot be attacked offline, and each session is independent, which gives forward secrecy so an attacker who later learns the passphrase cannot decrypt earlier recorded traffic. For open networks it adds opportunistic encryption that protects traffic between a client and the access point without requiring a shared password. Enterprise deployments gain a stricter optional mode using stronger cryptography for sensitive environments, and management frame protection is required rather than optional, which blunts forged disassociation attacks. In practice it shows up as a mode on access points, often run alongside WPA2 in a transition mode so older clients still connect. The mistake people usually make is assuming the WPA3 label means the whole network is strong: transition mode, weak passphrases, and unpatched clients that fall back to older protocols can all leave the same practical weakness in place.

beginner.definition: WPA3 is a newer and safer standard for protecting Wi-Fi networks. WPA is short for Wi-Fi Protected Access. It makes the secret code between your device and the router much harder to guess.
beginner.whyItMatters: Older Wi-Fi protection let an attacker record the login exchange and guess the password later. WPA3 removes that trick. It also protects each session on its own. So old recorded traffic stays private even if the password is later found.
howItWorks: You type the Wi-Fi password on your device as usual.
Your device and the router run a special exchange that never sends the password.
Each side proves it knows the password by solving the same puzzle.
The exchange produces a fresh secret key for this session only.
Your traffic is encrypted with that key and the key is then discarded.
The router also signs management messages so fakes are easier to spot.
beginner.example: Think of two people proving they know the same secret handshake. They perform it in front of each other and both recognise it. Nobody watching can copy it or use it later. Even a filmed handshake will not let a stranger into the club.
takeaways: WPA3 stops attackers from guessing a captured Wi-Fi password offline.
Each session gets its own key, so old traffic stays private.
A long, hard-to-guess Wi-Fi password still matters a great deal.

objectives: Explain what WPA3 is and which weakness in WPA2 it addresses.
Describe how a password-authenticated exchange avoids sending the passphrase.
Explain forward secrecy in simple terms for recorded wireless traffic.
Recognise the security trade-offs of running WPA3 in transition mode.
Identify client and configuration factors that limit WPA3's benefits.
